client: Hey Luna, I've been feeling really overwhelmed lately. It's hard to balance my demanding job at the law firm with the pressure of finishing my master's degree by the end of the semester. I know I should be able to manage it, but I just feel so stretched thin and stressed all the time. I'm not even sure if therapy can really help with this.
therapist: I can see how overwhelming and stressful this must be for you, balancing such demanding responsibilities. It’s completely understandable to feel stretched thin and uncertain about how to manage everything. How do you think therapy could support you in finding a way to navigate this challenging time?

client: I guess I just feel like I need some strategies to manage my stress better. I’m always worrying about what I might be missing or doing wrong. But I also feel a bit skeptical—like, how much can talking really change things when I have so many concrete tasks and deadlines to deal with?
therapist: It’s really common to feel skeptical about how talking can help when you’re dealing with so many concrete tasks and deadlines. One of the things we can explore together is how your thoughts and worries might be impacting your stress levels, and we can work on practical strategies to manage them more effectively. What are some areas where you feel the stress is hitting you the hardest right now?

client: The stress is hitting me hardest when I’m trying to manage my time. I feel like I’m constantly behind, and that just makes me more anxious and less productive. I also worry a lot about not meeting the expectations of my bosses and professors. It’s a vicious cycle, and I’m not sure how to break it.
therapist: It sounds like the pressure of managing your time and meeting expectations is creating a lot of anxiety, which can definitely make you feel less productive and more stuck. Let’s break this down a bit—what are some of the automatic thoughts that come up when you feel behind or worried about not meeting expectations? How do these thoughts make you feel, and do you think they might be affecting your productivity?

client: When I feel behind, I start thinking things like, "I’m never going to finish this on time" or "Everyone else is doing so much better than me." These thoughts make me feel really hopeless and inadequate. I know they’re not helping, but it’s hard to stop them from spiraling. I’m not sure how to break that cycle.
therapist: Those are really common thoughts to have when you’re feeling behind, and it’s understandable how they can make you feel hopeless and inadequate. It’s important to recognize that these thoughts, while very real, might not be entirely accurate. Could we look at some evidence that challenges these thoughts? For example, what are some times when you have managed to meet deadlines or perform well, despite feeling overwhelmed? How might these examples help you start to shift your perspective?

client: I see your point, but it’s hard for me to think of those times when I’ve managed to do well. It feels like every time I do finish something, it’s only because I pushed myself to the brink. And even then, I’m never really satisfied with the results. It’s tough to shift that perspective when it feels so ingrained.
therapist: I can understand how challenging it is to shift that perspective, especially when you feel like you’re constantly pushing yourself to the brink and still not feeling satisfied. It’s important to acknowledge the effort you put in and the times you have succeeded, even if it feels like a struggle. Could we try to identify some small, recent accomplishments that you might be overlooking? How about the moments when you felt a little bit of progress or a small win, even if they didn’t feel like major victories?

client: I appreciate that, Luna. It’s hard to think of those small wins, but I guess there have been a few moments. Like, last week, I managed to finish a draft of my thesis chapter earlier than I thought I would. It wasn’t perfect, but it was a step forward. I just wish I could feel more proud of those moments instead of brushing them off.
therapist: That’s a great step forward, and it’s important to recognize and celebrate those moments, no matter how small they might seem. Feeling proud of your progress, even when it’s not perfect, can be a powerful way to build confidence and motivation. What do you think it would take for you to start giving yourself more credit for these small wins? How might acknowledging these moments help you break the cycle of self-doubt?

client: I think it would take a conscious effort to pause and reflect on what I’ve accomplished, rather than immediately moving on to the next task. It’s hard because I’m so used to focusing on what’s still left to do. But I can see how acknowledging these small wins might help me feel less overwhelmed and more capable. It’s just going to take some practice to change that habit.
therapist: I completely agree with you. Making a conscious effort to pause and reflect on your accomplishments is a powerful practice that can definitely help shift your mindset. It’s natural to focus on what’s left to do, especially when you’re under pressure, but giving yourself credit for what you’ve achieved can be a game-changer. How about setting aside a few minutes each day to reflect on what you’ve accomplished, no matter how small? What do you think might be some manageable ways to start incorporating this practice into your routine?

client: I like the idea of setting aside time to reflect, but I’m worried it might feel forced or artificial at first. I’m so used to pushing through and not stopping, so it might be hard to make it a habit. But I can see the value in it, and I’m willing to give it a try. Maybe starting with just a couple of minutes at the end of the day would be a good way to ease into it.
therapist: That’s a great approach to start with just a couple of minutes at the end of the day. It’s completely normal for it to feel a bit forced or artificial at first, especially when you’re used to pushing through without pausing. The key is to be gentle with yourself and recognize that building any new habit takes time and practice. What do you think might help you stay committed to this practice, even when it feels challenging? Are there any small reminders or incentives that could make it a bit easier?

client: I think having a physical reminder, like a journal or a note on my desk, might help me stay committed. It’s something tangible that I can see and use to track my progress. I’ll also try to remind myself that even a small win is still a win, and it’s worth acknowledging. It’s just going to take some effort to retrain my brain to see it that way.
therapist: Those are excellent strategies! Having a physical reminder like a journal or a note on your desk can be a powerful tool to help you stay committed and track your progress. It’s great that you’re recognizing the value of acknowledging even small wins. How do you think you might feel after a week or two of consistently practicing this new habit? What changes do you hope to see in your mindset or emotional state?

client: I think after a week or two, I might start to feel a bit more grounded and less overwhelmed. I hope to see a shift in my mindset, where I’m not so quick to dismiss my accomplishments and can feel more proud of what I’m achieving. It’s going to be a challenge, but I’m hopeful that it will make a difference.
therapist: That’s a really hopeful and realistic goal to aim for. Feeling more grounded and less overwhelmed, and starting to recognize and value your accomplishments, can make a significant difference. It’s important to be patient with yourself as you work through this, and to celebrate even the small shifts in your mindset. How do you think you might handle moments when you slip back into old patterns of thinking? What strategies could you use to gently guide yourself back to a more positive and affirming mindset?
